fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A flattened cell shaped like a quadrant of a circle divides into equal halves by a circular-arc anticlinal wall meeting the side and periphery at right angles, cutting off about 55° 22′ of the arc and starting about three-tenths of the radius from the centre, since this is the shortest bisecting wall.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: bisecting a quadrant: circular arc \perp side and periphery, cutting off 55^\circ 22' of the arc, starting \approx 0.3r from the centre

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. VIII: The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Now we find that a flattened cell which is approximately a quadrant of a circle invariably divides after the manner of Fig. 145, C, that is to say, by an approximately circular, _anticlinal_ wall

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter VIII, “The Forms of Tissues, or Cell-Aggregates (continued)”; topic “Division of a flattened quadrant cell”. Scope: flattened discoid algae (e.g. Erythrotrichia) and eggs flattened under pressure (frog, sea-urchin) at the eight-cell stage

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: bisecting a quadrant: circular arc \perp side and periphery, cutting off 55^\circ 22' of the arc, starting \approx 0.3r from the centre

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch08-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: This is an unusually precise geometric law with clear confirming values. Existing imagery likely provides restricted examples, but not a broad, purpose-built sample spanning algae and pressure-flattened eggs.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Identify quadrant-shaped pre-division cells and measure daughter areas, wall curvature, endpoint angles, arc angle, and radial start position against the stated shortest-bisector solution.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Quadrant-shaped cells matching the assumptions are uncommon.

Flattening pressure and 3D thickness are often undocumented.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predicted arc is specific enough that a modest set of quadrant cells would confirm or refute it. Those cells are not available as an open morphometric dataset, though published figures show the qualitative anticlinal curve. The quantitative constants are only partly checkable from existing images.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: On quadrant-shaped flat cells, measure where the anticlinal wall meets the straight sides and what angle of arc it cuts off. An arc that meets both edges at right angles, cuts off about 55 degrees, and starts near three-tenths of the radius would support the claim; a straight radial wall or a periclinal wall in equal halves would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Erythrotrichia discs and pressure-flattened frog or sea-urchin eggs are illustrated in classical plates, not in a public coordinate table.

The numerical arc and radius fractions need measured outlines rather than schematic drawings.
